title: Kubernetes Probes, Resources, HPA and Pod Troubleshooting
summary: Quick revision notes on liveness, readiness and startup probes, resource requests and limits, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, and diagnosing CrashLoopBackOff, Pending and ImagePullBackOff.

chapters.title: Probes and Resources: The Mental Model
points: Probes are kubelet health checks on a container. Requests and limits are the scheduler's and kernel's resource contract. HPA changes the replica count. Together they decide whether a pod is placed, kept alive and sent traffic.

Liveness failure: kubelet restarts the container. Readiness failure: the pod is removed from Service endpoints but not restarted. Startup probe: holds off liveness and readiness until the app has booted.
Probe handlers: httpGet (2xx/3xx passes), tcpSocket (port opens), exec (exit code 0), grpc. Each probe runs on its own periodSeconds timer.
Requests are what the scheduler reserves when placing the pod. Limits are enforced at runtime: CPU is throttled, memory over the limit is OOMKilled.
Interview Point: What is the difference between liveness and readiness? Which probe protects a slow-starting app? What happens to traffic when readiness fails?

chapters.title: Configuring Probes Correctly
points: Key fields: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds (default 10), timeoutSeconds (default 1), successThreshold (default 1), failureThreshold (default 3).
Startup probe budget = failureThreshold x periodSeconds. For example, failureThreshold 30 and periodSeconds 10 gives the app 300s to start.
Comparison: liveness asks 'should I restart?', readiness asks 'should I get traffic?', startup asks 'has it finished booting?'. Only readiness gates the Service endpoints.
Example: readinessProbe: httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3.

Mistakes: a liveness probe that checks a database or other dependency causes cascading restarts; a liveness probe with a short timeout on a slow app causes restart loops; use a startup probe instead of a big initialDelaySeconds.
Interview Point: Why should liveness never check downstream dependencies? How do you size a startup probe? What is the default failureThreshold?

chapters.title: Requests, Limits and QoS Classes
points: CPU is in cores or millicores (500m = 0.5 core) and is compressible: over the limit means throttling. Memory is in Mi/Gi and is incompressible: over the limit means OOMKilled (exit code 137).

QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests = limits for every container, CPU and memory), Burstable (at least one request or limit set), BestEffort (none set). Under node pressure, BestEffort pods are evicted first, then Burstable.
Scheduling uses requests only. A pod stays Pending if no node has enough unreserved allocatable capacity.
Example: resources: {requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi}, limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}}.

Mistakes: no requests leaves HPA unable to compute CPU utilization; a CPU limit that is too low causes silent latency from throttling; a memory limit below the real working set causes repeated OOMKills.
Interview Point: Why is CPU throttled but memory killed? How does Kubernetes pick which pod to evict? What do requests affect that limits do not?

chapters.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
points: HPA formula: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetric / targetMetric). It checks about every 15s and needs metrics-server installed.
CPU utilization is measured against the pod's requests, not its limits. A pod with no CPU request cannot be scaled on CPU percentage.
Example: kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10, or an autoscaling/v2 HorizontalPodAutoscaler with minReplicas, maxReplicas and a metrics list.
Scale-down is slowed by a stabilization window (default 300s) to avoid flapping. Scale-up reacts faster. Tune it with spec.behavior.
Comparison: HPA adds or removes pods, VPA changes pod requests and limits, Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when pods are Pending.
Interview Point: How is the desired replica count calculated? Why does HPA show <unknown> for the metric? How do HPA and Cluster Autoscaler work together?

chapters.title: Troubleshooting CrashLoopBackOff, Pending and ImagePullBackOff
points: CrashLoopBackOff: the container starts, exits, and kubelet restarts it with exponential backoff (10s, 20s, 40s, up to 5 minutes). Check kubectl logs --previous, the exit code (1 app error, 137 OOMKilled/SIGKILL, 143 SIGTERM), and whether the liveness probe is killing it.
Pending: the pod is not scheduled. kubectl describe pod shows the Events, such as 0/3 nodes available: Insufficient cpu, untolerated taints, node selector or affinity mismatch, or an unbound PVC.
ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull: a wrong image name or tag, a missing imagePullSecrets entry for a private registry, or registry rate limits. Verify the image reference first.
Triage order: kubectl get pod, then kubectl describe pod (read the Events at the bottom), then kubectl logs (--previous for crashed containers), then kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp.

Mistakes: reading only the current logs of a restarting pod instead of --previous; guessing resource values instead of checking kubectl top pod; forgetting that a readiness failure shows as 0/1 Ready with no restarts.
Interview Point: A pod is Pending: what do you check first? How do you tell OOMKilled from an application crash? Why does ImagePullBackOff back off instead of failing?

chapters.title: Probes, Resources, HPA and Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet
points: Probes: liveness restarts, readiness gates traffic, startup protects slow boots. Startup budget = failureThreshold x periodSeconds.
Resources: scheduler uses requests, kernel enforces limits. CPU over limit is throttled, memory over limit is OOMKilled (137). QoS: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort.
HPA: ceil(current x currentMetric / target), needs metrics-server and CPU requests, scale-down window is 300s by default. kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10.
Debug commands: kubectl describe pod X, kubectl logs X --previous, kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp, kubectl top pod.

Status to cause: CrashLoopBackOff means the app or liveness probe is killing the container, Pending means no schedulable node or unbound PVC, ImagePullBackOff means a bad image name or missing pull secret.
Interview Point: Walk through debugging a pod that is not serving traffic. Which status points to scheduling and which to the container?
